title: `-0.0` in arithmetic: two zeros
description: Arithmetic keeps the sign of zero: `1.0 / -0.0` is -inf, `-(0.0)` and `0.0 * -1` are -0.0, `sqrt(-0.0)` is -0.0. Comparison, grouping and sorting are in polars-zero-order.

With a literal operand on a frame of two rows or more, the kernels take shortcuts that move the sign of a zero away from IEEE: `x + 0.0` and `x - 0.0` return `x`, so `-0.0 + 0.0` and `-0.0 - (-0.0)` are -0.0 (IEEE gives 0.0), and `0.0 - x` is `-x`, so `0.0 - 0.0` is -0.0. Two columns use the IEEE operations.

provenance.notes: `sverify_dev.probe_polars` runs each expression on edge cases (0, ±1, ±2, 3, ±7, the bounds of the integer width; 0.5, ±2.5, 7, 1e308, ±inf, NaN; NULL), one row at a time, and compares each row with Lean's outcome of the Substrait call under each candidate option (`substrait-check --outcomes`). Observations are Polars programs whose result is recorded as it is. Polars 2.1.0 (Python), Rust crates at tag py-2.1.0 (commit 7f902bd3), on macOS arm64.

evidence.note: The same section at tag py-2.1.0.

provenance.notes: Polars's user guide says it generally follows IEEE 754 for `Float32` and `Float64`, with two exceptions: any NaN equals any other NaN and is greater than every non-NaN value, and operations guarantee nothing about the sign of zero or NaN or a NaN's payload (a sort or group by may make every zero +0 and every NaN a positive NaN). It promises no error bound unless a function says otherwise. The user guide is not versioned; the section reads the same at tag py-2.1.0. So the two zeros the probes show are what Polars 2.1.0 happens to do: the docs do not promise them, and a sort or group by may turn `-0.0` into `0.0`. The `Float32` rows stay open.

evidence.note: The column kernels: `-x`, `l + r`, `l - r`, `l * r`, `l / r`.
The literal kernels: `x + 0` and `x - 0` return `x`, `0 - x` is `-x`, `x * ±1` is `x` or `-x`.
`+ - * // %` on two ChunkedArrays: equal lengths take the array kernel, a length-1 side the scalar kernel.
A literal is a scalar column, passed to the operation as a one-value Series.
The streaming engine evaluates each expression with polars-expr's `PhysicalExpr` on every morsel, so it runs the same kernels.

notes: `impl_float_arith_kernel!` is one macro instantiated for `pf16`, `f32` and `f64`, so `Float32` and `Float64` run the same operations. The streaming engine evaluates expressions through polars-expr on each morsel (`StreamExpr` in crates/polars-stream/src/expression.rs), so it shares these kernels with the in-memory engine. The column kernels are the IEEE operations, so `Float32` keeps two zeros as `Float64` does.

The kernels for a literal operand take shortcuts that move the sign of a zero away from IEEE, at both widths: `x + 0.0` and `x - 0.0` return `x` unchanged, so `-0.0 + 0.0` and `-0.0 - (-0.0)` are -0.0 (IEEE gives 0.0), and `0.0 - x` is `-x`, so `0.0 - 0.0` is -0.0. A literal is a length-1 column, so the shortcut runs on frames of two rows or more; on one row both sides have length 1 and the column kernel runs.
Read at tag py-2.1.0 (commit 7f902bd3). The streaming engine evaluates expressions through polars-expr on each morsel (crates/polars-stream/src/expression.rs), so these kernels serve both engines.

evidence.note: pl.DataFrame({'x': [49.0, 3.0, -0.0, 0.0, 0.5]}).select(a=pl.col('x') + 0.0, s=pl.col('x') - (-0.0), l=pl.lit(0.0) - pl.col('x')) gave a = -0.0 and s = -0.0 for x = -0.0, and l = -0.0 for x = 0.0 (Polars 2.1.0, macOS arm64).

notes: Adds the second paragraph of the description: the literal shortcuts for `x + 0`, `x - 0` and `0 - x`, read in the source and seen in the manual repro of this round.

In memory, s-zero-sign-literal shows the shortcuts on 4 rows and on 6000. Streaming takes them only in morsels of two rows or more: polars-zero-sign-streaming, which supersedes this fact for the streaming engine.
